title: Committee of Supply – Head P (Ministry of Home Affairs)
what_it_is: Committee of Supply – Head P (Ministry of Home Affairs)

sections.label: Jakarta bombings and MHA challenges
sections.summary: The Jakarta bombings and rounding up of 27 Bangladeshi workers prompt a question on MHA's present and future challenges.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The Jakarta bombings and the rounding up of 27 Bangladeshi foreign workers in January are sobering reminders of this new reality.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In light of this, could the Minister provide an assessment of the key challenges faced by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) at present and those that it anticipates to arise in the near future?

sections.label: SG Secure measures for unity
sections.summary: A question asks what measures under SG Secure will unite Singaporeans and safeguard the social fabric.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In light of the recent announcement regarding the launch of SG Secure by the Minister for Home Affairs just last month, it is heartening to know that the Government recognises the importance of the community's response to a potential attack.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Could the Minister elaborate on what measures are being contemplated under SG Secure to unite Singaporeans and to safeguard 	Page: 46 the social fabric that we have so carefully and deliberately woven together as a nation?

sections.label: Emerging stronger and united
sections.summary: The passage states Singaporeans must emerge stronger and united, and that SG Secure recognises a whole-of-society approach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And in the event that such threats do materialise, we have to emerge stronger, more united and more determined as Singaporeans and to fight back as one united Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It is good that SG Secure recognises that security is about a whole-of-society approach and mindset.

sections.label: Highest terror threat level
sections.summary: The threat of a terror attack on Singapore soil is at its highest level ever.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The threat of a terror attack on our soil is at the highest level that it has ever been.

sections.label: Welcome for SG Secure community role
sections.summary: The speaker welcomes SG Secure, which involves the community and empowers groups to help Singapore stay alert, united and strong.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In particular, I welcome the introduction of SG Secure which involves the community; where different groups of Singaporeans will be empowered and enabled to help Singapore stay alert, united and strong.

sections.label: SG Secure and multiracial sensitivities
sections.summary: A question asks the Ministry to elaborate on SG Secure initiatives and measures to manage multiracial and multi-religious sensitivities in counter-terrorism messaging.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: This may be an opportunity to learn more about each other and foster stronger bonds to counter terrorism together.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Ministry to elaborate on the key initiatives of SG Secure and whether there will be specific measures that will be taken to preserve and manage multiracial and multi-religious sensitivities in counter-terrorism messaging.

sections.label: ISIS Southeast Asian arm Katibah Nusantara
sections.summary: The Prime Minister alluded on his US trip that ISIS has a battalion-size Southeast Asian arm called Katibah Nusantara.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Prime Minister, in his recent trip to the US, alluded to the fact that ISIS has a battalion-size Southeast Asian arm called Katibah Nusantara.

sections.label: Katibah Nusantara threat and MHA
sections.summary: The question asks the Minister for details on Katibah Nusantara's evolution and threat, its impact on MHA, and differences from Jemaah Islamiyah.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can the Minister share details about the evolution and threat posed by Katibah Nusantara and other groups aligned to ISIS and how it has impacted upon MHA's work and if there have been any differences in approach in dealing with such groups from the Jemaah Islamiyah experience?

sections.label: Crimes per 100,000 KPI
sections.summary: One KPI is overall crimes per 100,000 population, which reflects only crimes reported to and recorded by the Police.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: One of the KPIs is the number of overall crimes per 100,000 population.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I would caution that this figure simply reflects the incidence of crimes reported to and recorded by the Police.

sections.label: Uncovering unreported crime
sections.summary: A more accurate picture of Singapore's crime situation requires attempting to uncover unreported crime.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If the Ministry wishes to have a more accurate picture of the crime situation in Singapore, there needs to be an attempt to uncover unreported crime.

sections.label: SPF officer to population ratio
sections.summary: SPF functions at about 170 officers per 100,000 population and leverages technology, outsourcing and civilianising jobs to cope.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Currently, SPF is functioning at probably a very low police officer to population ratio of 170 officers per 100,000 population, and it is trying to leverage on technology, outsourcing and civilianising jobs to cope.

sections.label: Malaysians to Singaporeans ratio claim
sections.summary: An officer said the allowed ratio is five Malaysians to one Singaporean, and the speaker wonders if that is true.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: One officer recently told me that the ratio allowed is five Malaysians to one Singaporean and I wonder if that is true.

sections.label: Civilian recruitment and training
sections.summary: The speaker questions whether a case is isolated and asks what role the Government plays in selecting and training civilians deployed to face the public.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I do not know whether this gentleman's experience is an isolated incident or not.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, it raises the issue of how civilians are recruited and trained before they are deployed to face the public.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What role does the Government play in ensuring that such personnel are properly chosen and trained?

sections.label: Home Team manpower growth
sections.summary: Home Team manpower grew by 5,000 officers over a decade, from 19,300 to 24,700 in 2015, with plans to recruit 2,000 more.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Home Team manpower has only grown by 5,000 officers in the past decade, from 19,300 to 24,700 in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In the 2015 Budget, there were plans to recruit another 2,000 officers to the Home Team.

sections.label: Births from 2003 to 2005
sections.summary: Between 2003 and 2005, fewer than 37,500 births were recorded each year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Between 2003 and 2005, fewer than 37,500 births were recorded each year.

sections.label: Re-employing and recalling Police officers
sections.summary: The speaker suggests extending re-employment of Police officers beyond current retirement and pensionable ages and inviting back resigned ex-officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
sentences.text: First, I suggest we further extend the re-employment of Police officers from their current retirement and pensionable ages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
sentences.text: Second, we should invite back our ex-officers who have resigned and who may be keen to rejoin the service.

sections.label: Orders issued and SAFRA Punggol
sections.summary: Orders issued rose from 149 in 2010 to over 2,000 in 2015, and the new SAFRA Punggol Clubhouse opens tomorrow with enrichment centres and a jackpot facility.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The number of such orders issued rose from 149 in 2010 to well over 2,000 in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The new SAFRA Punggol Clubhouse will open tomorrow.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: It boasts five enrichment centres for children aged three to 16 years old, the biggest preschool with an enrolment of up to 120 children, children-friendly facilities and a jackpot facility that opens daily from 10.00 am to 1.00 am, and up to 3.00 am on Friday, Saturday and eve of public holidays.

sections.label: Jackpot licences at clubhouses
sections.summary: The speaker urges the Ministry to tighten control of jackpot licences for clubhouses, especially those housing preschools and enrichment centres under one roof.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: It is another thing to have children going to the same clubhouse almost every day for preschool and enrichment classes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: I urge the Ministry to exercise tighter control and management of jackpot licences for clubhouses, especially those with preschool and enrichment centre under one roof.

sections.label: Stateless people and NRIC misuse
sections.summary: The passage states this will stop some sellers using old NRIC addresses for criminal offences, and notes over 1,000 stateless people aged 50 and above.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: This will also stop some sellers from using their old NRIC address to commit criminal offences going forward.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: We have in our society over 1,000 stateless people aged 50 and above.

sections.label: Granting stateless residents citizenship
sections.summary: A man said citizenship would make his mother happy with a sense of belonging, and the speaker asks for compassion to grant 1,411 stateless residents citizenship.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Without hesitation, he said, "Yes, it will make my mother very happy because she will have a sense of belonging finally." Madam, could we not exercise a little more compassion as we embark to write the next chapter in our history and grant these stateless residents − 1,411 to be exact − the citizenship they so rightly deserve?

sections.label: Number of stateless persons
sections.summary: The Minister for Home Affairs said that as of January 2016 there were 1,411 stateless persons living in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In response to a recent Parliamentary Question, the Minister for Home Affairs shared that, as of January 2016, there were 1,411 stateless persons living in Singapore.

sections.label: Stateless citizenship applications and outcomes
sections.summary: Between 2003 and 2012 about 500 to 600 stateless persons applied yearly, about 91% eventually obtained citizenship, but many born in Singapore still cannot.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In 2013, it was revealed that between 2003 and 2012, about 500 to 600 stateless persons applied for Singapore citizenship every year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: While about 91% of these applications were successful in eventually obtaining Singapore citizenship, there are still many stateless persons born in Singapore who fall through the cracks and are unable to obtain Singapore citizenship.

sections.label: Inmate training and work programme numbers
sections.summary: Singapore Prison Service statistics show inmates in training programmes dropped by 345 from 2014 to 2015, and only 81% of employable inmates were in work programmes in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: According to statistics from the Singapore Prison Service, the number of inmates engaged in training programmes dropped by 345 from 2014 to 2015.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The SCORE annual report notes that of the inmates deemed 	Page: 55 employable in 2014, only 81% were engaged in work programmes.

sections.label: Estimated recidivism rate rise
sections.summary: The 2016 Budget Book estimates recidivism will rise to 28% in 2016 from 26.8% in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In the 2016 Budget Book, recidivism, the percentage of discharged criminal offenders who go on to re-offend, is estimated to rise to 28% in 2016, from 26.8% in 2015.

sections.label: Social impact bonds for ex-offenders
sections.summary: The speaker suggests examining social impact bonds to fund programmes that rehabilitate ex-offenders and reduce recidivism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, I suggest we examine the role that social impact bonds can play in funding innovative programmes that help rehabilitate ex-offenders into society and keep recidivism at bay.

sections.label: Social impact bond for rehabilitation
sections.summary: The speaker urges the Home Team to consider a social impact bond, noting Australian and US examples and over 60% repeat drug offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: States in Australia and the US have launched or planned to launch social impact bonds around this theme as well.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I urge the Home Team to consider issuing a social impact bond to better target funds and spur innovation for rehabilitation and anti-recidivism programmes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
sentences.text: In the past three years, over 60% of drug abusers arrested are repeat offenders.

sections.label: Rehabilitation and employability of ex-drug offenders
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether plans exist to improve rehabilitation at DRCs and ex-drug offenders' employability after release.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
sentences.text: I fully appreciate that it is difficult to fight their addiction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
sentences.text: However, with such high numbers of repeat offenders, are there any plans to improve the rehabilitation process at our DRCs and the 	Page: 56 employability of ex-drug offenders when they are released?

sections.label: Mandatory Aftercare and spent records
sections.summary: The Mandatory Aftercare Scheme and 2005 Registration of Criminals Act amendments facilitate reintegration and prevent spent records from prejudicing the future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: For example, the introduction of the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme under the amended Prisons Act has facilitated the gradual rehabilitation and reintegration of released persons back into society after their release.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Similarly, the amendments to the Registration of Criminals Act in 2005 – to allow released persons, who have criminal records that had been spent, to be deemed to have no record of their conviction – prevents their past mistakes from prejudicing their future.

sections.label: Ex-offender placement rate and employment
sections.summary: The speaker asks SCORE and Singapore Prison Service for the past five years' placement rate and what MHA does for ex-offender employment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
sentences.text: Can SCORE and the Singapore Prison Service share what is the placement rate of ex-offenders the past five years when they are released from incarceration?

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
sentences.text: I ask this because, with a very tight labour market situation and as we look at how to minimise our unemployment rate, what more is MHA doing to help in the employment facilitation of these ex-offenders!

sections.label: Update on SCORE programme
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister for an update on how the SCORE programme is helping offenders.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
sentences.text: Can the Minister give an update on how the SCORE programme is helping offenders?

sections.label: Youth drug abuse rising
sections.summary: Youth drug abuse cases are increasing, with almost 70% of new drug abusers arrested in 2015 below age 30, and ice and heroin most commonly abused.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The number of cases of youth drug abuse has been increasing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In 2015, almost 70% of the new drug abusers arrested were below the age of 30. "Ice" or methamphetamine and heroin are the most commonly abused drugs. "Ice" is more popular amongst young drug abusers who have the misconception that it is less harmful and less addictive than heroin.

sections.label: CNB 2015 tolerant attitudes
sections.summary: The 2015 CNB report noted signs of increasingly tolerant attitudes towards drugs, especially amongst youths.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: According to the CNB report in 2015, there have been signs of an increasingly tolerant attitude towards drugs, especially amongst youths.

sections.label: Singapore drug situation and cannabis
sections.summary: CNB keeps Singapore's drug situation under control, but nearly 70% of new abusers are below 30 and cannabis is the second most abused drug among first-timers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: Thanks to CNB, the drug situation in Singapore is under control.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: However, amongst new drug abusers, nearly 70% are below the age of 30.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: According to CNB, cannabis has become the second most abused drug amongst first-time drug abusers.

sections.label: Minister asked on task force
sections.summary: The question asks the Minister how the Ministry implemented the Task Force on youths and drugs recommendations and what further steps it intends.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Could the Minister outline how the Ministry has implemented the recommendations of the Task Force on youths and drugs in the past year and what further steps, if any, that the Ministry intends to take to arrest the increase in the number of new and young drug 	Page: 59 abusers in Singapore?

sections.label: Young cannabis abusers' views
sections.summary: In January 2016 the Minister noted rising cannabis abusers, over half arrested below 30, and a study showing young abusers viewed cannabis as a soft drug.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Further, in January 2016, the Minister for Home Affairs had noted in this House that there had been a worrying trend of a rising number of cannabis abusers in Singapore, with more than half of those arrested below 30 years of age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: He had highlighted a study done that showed that many young cannabis abusers held the view that "cannabis is a soft drug, and that the harms and addictiveness of cannabis were less serious than tobacco".

sections.label: 2015 crime rate rise
sections.summary: SPF's Annual Crime Brief 2015 reported overall crime rose 4%, largely due to online commercial crimes rising 46.5% from 2014 to 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: In the Annual Crime Brief 2015 released by SPF in February 2016, it was reported that the overall crime rate in Singapore increased by 4%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: This has been credited largely to the rise in online commercial crimes which increased by a troubling 46.5% from 2014 to 2015, with almost all other 	Page: 60 classes of crime registering a decrease in the number of cases.

sections.label: Government partnerships against transnational cybercrime
sections.summary: The Government needs to work with INTERPOL and ASEAN members to detect and deal with transnational cybercrimes, giving the Home Team capabilities and resources.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: To address this, there is a need for the Government to work closely with international organisations like INTERPOL and other ASEAN members to effectively detect and deal with transnational cybercrimes in the region.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: These partnerships will provide our Home Team with the capabilities to deal with cross-border crimes more effectively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Ultimately, we must ensure that the Home Team has the resources, wherewithal, capabilities and drive to deal with cybercrime effectively, especially those crimes with cross-border elements or cross-border accomplices.

sections.label: Online scam cases and anti-scam campaign
sections.summary: Online credit-for-sex scam cases rose 1,723% and internet love scams 93.4%, prompting an NCPC and Police anti-scam campaign whose impact and enhancements are questioned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: Last year, online credit-for-sex scam cases increased 1,723%, resulting in a loss of $2.9 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: Internet love scams increased by 93.4%, resulting in a loss of $12 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: The National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC) and the Police have launched a nationwide anti-scam public education campaign, with roadshows, exhibitions and commercials.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: How would the Ministry assess the impact of this campaign and what enhancements are needed to stem the tide?

sections.label: Little India congestion suggestions
sections.summary: The speaker asks for the Minister's update and consideration of five suggestions on Little India congestion, including a task force, ring-fencing communal areas and stakeholder dialogues.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I, hence, wish to ask for the Minister's update of his plans in regard to this matter.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I also ask for his favourable consideration of the following suggestions: (a) Form a high-level multi-agency task force to mitigate the security and dis-amenity risks of high congestion of visitors to Little India; (b) Ring-fence the communal areas of residents, such as the playgrounds and void decks so that the old and the young get to use the space meant for them; (c) Continue with and do not stop resourcing the recommendations of the Committee of Inquiry viz-a-viz alcohol consumption restrictions and patrol teams; (d) Decentralise further by building more recreation centres outside Little India; and (e) Engage regularly, through planned dialogues, with all key stakeholders, the foreign workers, agents, businesses and residents.

sections.label: Unlicensed moneylending at 10-year low
sections.summary: The unlicensed moneylending situation hit a 10-year low.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The unlicensed moneylending situation hit a 10-year low.

sections.label: Singapore ranked first in Gallup report
sections.summary: The 2015 Gallup Global Law and Order Report ranked Singapore first out of 141 countries.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Globally, the 2015 Gallup Global Law and Order Report ranked Singapore first out of 141 countries.

sections.label: Terrorism threat and ISIS
sections.summary: The Minister says he has explained the terrorism threat, including that ISIS poses a far graver threat than Al Qaeda in scale, network, finances and propaganda.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Moving on to the topic of terrorism, Mr Singh asked about the nature of the threat of terrorism.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I have explained this in recent speeches on terrorism, including how, in terms of scale, network, finances and propaganda, ISIS poses a far graver threat than Al Qaeda ever was.

sections.label: Counter-terrorism efforts enhancement
sections.summary: The Ministry will significantly enhance counter-terrorism efforts in three areas.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: My Ministry will significantly enhance our counter-terrorism efforts in three areas.

sections.label: New national movement SG Secure
sections.summary: A new national movement called SG Secure will strengthen the community response.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Three, strengthen our community response through a new national movement which we will call SG Secure.

sections.label: SG Secure builds on CEP
sections.summary: SG Secure will build on the foundation set by the Community Engagement Programme.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: SG Secure will build on the foundation we have set so far as part of the Community Engagement Programme (CEP).

sections.label: SG Secure scope and focus
sections.summary: SG Secure will be larger in scope and scale, focusing on vigilance and community response to threats.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: SG Secure will be larger in scope and scale in its outreach.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It will have a sharper focus on vigilance and on preparing the community to respond appropriately to potential threats.

sections.label: Radicalisation assessment and extremist teachings
sections.summary: The Home Team assesses radicalisation, and the line is drawn clearly on support for terrorist groups like ISIS.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Mr Singh also asked how the Home Team assesses if an individual has been radicalised and how Singaporeans can be inoculated against extremist teachings.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We draw the line quite clearly on support for terrorist groups like ISIS.

sections.label: Deported men possessed extremist material
sections.summary: The 27 deported men possessed material on silent killing, jihadist propaganda and how to engage in jihad.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The 27 men we deported possessed material on them on silent killing, on jihadist propaganda and how to engage in jihad.

sections.label: Detention and Restraining Orders
sections.summary: Singaporeans assessed as serious and imminent threats get Detention Orders under the Internal Security Act, while those with extremist leanings but far from acting may get Restraining Orders.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Supposing they were 27 Singaporeans, then we make distinctions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We look at who is likely to pose a serious and imminent threat and a Detention Order will be made under the Internal Security Act against them.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The rest ‒ and we have done that frequently over the years ‒ if we believe that they have extremist leanings but they are quite far removed from actually carrying out or doing something, we advise them, we may put them on a Restraining Order.

sections.label: Detainees held until rehabilitated
sections.summary: In Singapore, people picked up are assessed and not released until believed to have been rehabilitated.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In Singapore, when we pick them up, we make an assessment and we do not release them until we believe that they have been rehabilitated.

sections.label: Home Team intelligence and data tools
sections.summary: The Home Team will use all available intelligence and investigation tools and make better use of data such as public transport video cameras and the ERP system.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Home Team will use all intelligence and investigation tools available and make better use of available data, for example, public transport video cameras and the Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) system.

sections.label: Counter-terrorism MOU with Australia
sections.summary: In June 2015, Singapore signed a comprehensive MOU on counter-terrorism with Australia.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In June 2015, we signed a comprehensive MOU on counter-terrorism with Australia.

sections.label: Changi Airport traveller volume growth
sections.summary: At Changi Airport, traveller volume is expected to increase by up to 50% in 10 years, from 120,000 to 180,000 travellers per day.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: At Changi Airport, we expect the volume of travellers to increase by up to 50% in 10 years – from 120,000 per day to 180,000 travellers per day.

sections.label: Reported cases last year
sections.summary: Last year, 344 such cases were reported, about one case every single day.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Last year, 344 such cases were reported, about one case every single day.

sections.label: Police manning levels low
sections.summary: Singapore has 170 Police officers per 100,000 population, which is low compared to London, New York and Hong Kong.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: As it is, our overall manning levels are not high.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We only have 170 Police officers per 100,000 population, which is quite low, compared to other cities like London, New York and Hong Kong.

sections.label: Police cameras in HDB estates
sections.summary: SPF will invest to extend Police cameras to public areas in HDB residential estates, alongside ongoing talks on manpower caps.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This is going to require on-going conversations about our manpower caps, even as we increase the size of our ERTs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This year, SPF will be making a major investment to extend Police cameras to public areas in our HDB residential estates, such as town centres, neighbourhood centres and pedestrian walkways linking HDB blocks to bus interchanges and MRT stations.

sections.label: Automated clearance at motorcycle counters
sections.summary: By year-end, all motorcycle counters at land checkpoints will have automated clearance facilities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: By year-end, all motorcycle counters at our land checkpoints will be equipped with automated clearance facilities.

sections.label: Changi Airport Terminal 4 self-service
sections.summary: The new Changi Airport Terminal 4 will use more self-service immigration facilities powered by technology, reducing reliance on manpower.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Likewise, the new Changi Airport Terminal 4 will feature a new operating model with more self-service immigration facilities powered by technology and creating a hassle-free experience and reducing reliance on manpower.

sections.label: Police recruitment and unified rank structure
sections.summary: Police will step up recruitment for ERTs and Special Operations troops, and implement a unified rank structure.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Police will step up recruitment this year to fill new posts in its ERTs and to build up the Special Operations troops.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: First, Police will implement a unified rank structure, moving away from the separate schemes for junior officers and senior officers that we currently have.

sections.label: APOs performing core functions
sections.summary: Police can perform core functions like crime-fighting and countering terrorism, with about 7,000 APOs deployed in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Police then can perform core functions like crime-fighting and countering terrorism.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
